title: Kulko v. Superior Court of California
lead: A New York father accommodated his daughter’s wish to live with her mother in California; the ensuing support suit asked whether that family decision subjected him to California’s personal jurisdiction.

actors.name: Ezra Kulko
actors.role: New York father challenging California jurisdiction over increased support

actors.name: Sharon Kulko, later Horn
actors.role: Mother who moved to California and sought custody and increased support

actors.name: Ilsa and Darwin Kulko
actors.role: Children born and originally raised in New York

actors.name: Justice Brennan
actors.role: Dissenter joined by White and Powell

proceedings: California trial court denied motion to quash; state appellate courts upheld jurisdiction, with the California Supreme Court divided 4–2; U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari after dismissing the formal appeal and reversed 6–3.
limits: The support obligation required personal jurisdiction; California’s custody jurisdiction was not contested. The Court did not decide the amount of support owed. Reciprocal-support procedures are described as they existed in 1978.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The family’s life and agreement were centered in New York
sections.cue: Place the California wedding in its limited chronological role.
paragraphs: Ezra and Sharon Kulko were New York residents and domiciliaries. They married in California in 1959 during Ezra’s three-day military stopover en route to Korea. Sharon returned to New York, and Ezra returned there after military service and another brief California stopover. Their son Darwin was born in New York in 1961 and their daughter Ilsa in 1962. The family lived there until Ezra and Sharon separated in March 1972.

Sharon moved to San Francisco, but returned to New York to sign a September 1972 separation agreement. The children would live with Ezra during school terms and visit Sharon during specified vacations. Sharon waived her own support, and Ezra agreed to pay $3,000 annually for periods when the children were with her. Sharon then personally obtained a Haitian divorce incorporating the agreement; Ezra supplied a power of attorney. Sharon returned to California and remarried.

In December 1973, Ilsa told Ezra she wanted to remain in California after Christmas. Ezra agreed and bought her a one-way ticket. Ilsa thereafter spent school terms with Sharon and vacations with Ezra. In January 1976, Darwin asked Sharon to let him join her. Sharon sent Darwin a ticket without Ezra’s knowledge. Thus Ezra consented to Ilsa’s move but did not arrange Darwin’s.

sections.title: Sharon’s support action drew Ezra’s jurisdictional objection
sections.cue: Distinguish the obligation to pay from the custody proceeding.
paragraphs: Soon after Darwin arrived, Sharon sued in California to establish the Haitian decree as a California judgment, obtain full custody, and increase Ezra’s child support. Ezra appeared specially and moved to quash service for lack of personal jurisdiction. He did not challenge California’s authority to decide custody. His objection concerned the personal obligation to pay increased support.

The trial court denied his motion, and Ezra sought a writ of mandate. California’s appellate courts upheld jurisdiction. The California Supreme Court, divided 4–2, treated Ezra’s consent to Ilsa’s move as an out-of-state act producing California effects. It reasoned that he purposefully obtained California’s laws and services through Ilsa’s presence, benefited from reduced household expenses, and could reasonably be required to defend there. On that basis, it sustained support jurisdiction for both children.

The U.S. Supreme Court dismissed the formal appeal but treated Ezra’s papers as a certiorari petition and granted review. Ezra disputed the exercise of jurisdiction, rather than properly attacking California’s statute, which reached only constitutional limits. Sharon argued that his later request to continue proceedings waived the objection, but the cited California cases did not establish waiver and the trial court still called his appearance special. Intervening orders on arrears and increased support did not eliminate the live jurisdictional issue.

sections.title: The majority found accommodation, not purposeful California activity
sections.cue: Explain why the asserted benefits did not supply contacts.
paragraphs: Justice Marshall’s six-Justice majority held that California lacked the minimum contacts necessary to impose this support obligation on Ezra. Notice was adequate; the problem was whether the nature and quality of Ezra’s own connection made jurisdiction fair and reasonable. His brief military stopovers and wedding did not support this unrelated later action.

The original vacation arrangement did not supply the connection either. California’s highest court had not relied on it, and treating consent to visits as purposeful forum activity could discourage sensible arrangements and expose a parent to suit wherever the other parent moved. Mailing support payments likewise contemplated any address Sharon might designate, rather than a deliberately California-centered undertaking.

Ezra’s accommodation of Ilsa’s preference served family harmony; it was not an effort to obtain California’s legal benefits for himself. Schools, hospitals, and other services primarily benefited Ilsa. Reduced household costs resulted from her absence from New York, not specifically from her presence in California. Whether Ezra consequently owed more support could be litigated in New York, but that merits question did not determine the proper forum.

sections.title: Effects and the state’s interests could not replace the missing connection
sections.cue: Address the alternative theories and available enforcement route.
paragraphs: California had invoked the effects approach in Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws § 37. Marshall explained that the provision addressed wrongful outside conduct causing in-state injury or commercial activity affecting residents, subject to reasonableness. Ezra had caused no comparable physical injury and sought no California commercial advantage. The dispute arose from a New York separation and an agreement negotiated and signed there. Consenting to a child’s move differed from an insurer soliciting a California policyholder.

Ezra remained in the marital domicile while Sharon moved across the country. Requiring him to defend roughly 3,000 miles away because he cooperated with Ilsa’s wishes would burden family relations. Making jurisdiction depend on whether he bought the ticket or unsuccessfully resisted the move could punish cooperative parenting. That concern held regardless of the merits of Sharon’s demand for additional support.

California had a substantial interest in resident children, but that interest alone did not establish jurisdiction over Ezra. The possible applicability of California law was also distinct from adjudicative power. Reciprocal-support statutes provided another route: Sharon could begin in California, have the matter sent to a responding New York court with jurisdiction over Ezra, and seek adjudication and collection there without either parent necessarily traveling to the other state. California used the revised 1968 uniform statute; New York used a similar earlier scheme.

sections.title: A close dissent did not change the limited reversal
sections.cue: State both the disagreement and what the judgment left open.
paragraphs: Justice Brennan, joined by Justices White and Powell, dissented. He accepted the majority’s minimum-contacts standard and considered the application close, but independently weighed the circumstances as sufficient to make California jurisdiction fair and reasonable. His brief opinion did not announce jurisdiction wherever a child happens to reside.

On May 15, 1978, the Supreme Court reversed the California Supreme Court because Ezra’s motion to quash on the support issue had been wrongly denied. The 6–3 decision did not extinguish the children’s right to support, set the amount Ezra owed, or disturb the uncontested question of custody jurisdiction.
